lead: A flexible drive carries power from one shaft to another through a belt, chain or rope that bends around pulleys or sprockets. Because the member bends, the shafts can sit far apart and need only rough alignment, which a gear pair cannot do. Belts grip by friction and allow a little slip, which soaks up shock; chains and timing belts grip by teeth or rollers and hold the speed ratio exact. Belts, chains and wire ropes run mills, conveyors, motorcycles, lifts and generator sets across Indian plants.
prereq: You need: density, material properties and the factor of safety from the design foundations, and shaft design for the shaft that carries the pulley load. The tension and width calculation of the belt itself follows in design of flat belt drives.

blocks.text: A flexible drive has three parts: a driving pulley or sprocket on the input shaft, a driven one on the output shaft, and one continuous member wrapped round both. Torque enters at the driving pulley, travels along the member as tension, and leaves as torque at the driven shaft. The small pulley is often, but not always, the driver. Nothing rigid connects the shafts, so they can sit a metre or ten metres apart and be out of line by a degree or two without stopping the drive.

The members divide by how they grip. Flat, V and round belts grip by friction on the pulley and slip a little when overloaded. Timing belts have moulded teeth that mesh with grooves in the pulley; chains have rollers that seat in sprocket teeth. Neither of those slips. Wire and fibre ropes carry load only in tension and run on drums or large sheaves.

Against a gear pair the trade is clear. Gears give an exact velocity ratio in a small rigid box, but need a short centre distance, accurate alignment, continuous lubrication and a sealed casing. A flexible drive is cheap and tolerant of misalignment; belt drives are also quiet and absorb shock, while chain and timing-belt drives are noisier and pass shock through more readily. In exchange you pay in slip (belts), extra shaft bending load and floor space.

Leather is the oldest belt material and still the textbook reference. Hides are oak-tanned — tanned with tannin from bark — which makes them tough and slightly stiff. Standard design values: density about 1000 kg/m³, and coefficient of friction μ = 0.25 to 0.4 for leather on a cast-iron pulley. Leather takes high tensile stress and runs quietly, but it stretches with use, loses strength when wet, and needs occasional dressing with a friction compound.

Cotton canvas, woven into a heavy cloth called duck and bonded with rubber, makes the common rubber flat belt. Several plies of canvas carry the load; the rubber holds them together and gives the friction face. Balata, a gum from a tropical tree, impregnates cotton belting to make it waterproof with a high, steady grip; it softens above about 40 °C, so it suits cool, damp places.

High-strength belts use synthetic cords. Nylon is strong and absorbs shock but stretches; polyester is stiffer and holds its length; aramid cord gives very high strength with low stretch where the belt must be narrow and fast. The cover is rubber or polyurethane, chosen for grip and resistance to oil and grit.

A flat belt is a stack of layers. Tension cords carry the pull and sit as close as possible to the neutral axis — the plane inside the belt that neither stretches nor shortens when the belt bends. Above and below the cords sit compression rubber and fabric plies, with a cover on each face for friction and to keep oil out. Cords near the neutral axis see little bending stress, so the belt runs on a small pulley without fatigue.

A flat belt must be joined into a loop. A skived and cemented joint (ends cut to a taper, glued and pressed) runs smoothly and keeps most of the belt strength. Metal lacing threaded through punched holes is quick to fit but heavier and weaker, and slaps at every pulley; hinged wire hooks serve for temporary repairs. The joint is the weakest section, so the allowable tension is reduced by a joint efficiency.

V-belts are moulded endless, with a trapezoidal cross-section and a layer of tension cord just under the top face. Standard sections run A, B, C, D and E, with top widths from about 13 mm (A) up to 38 mm (E); each section covers a range of pulley diameters and powers. The belt itself has an included angle of 40°, and the pulley groove is cut a little narrower, 34° to 38°, so the belt always bears on its two sides. Small pulleys get the narrowest groove: when the belt bends round a small radius, its stretched top narrows and its squeezed bottom widens, so its side angle drops below 40°.
T<sub>c</sub> = m v², where m = ρ b t
blocks.where: T<sub>c</sub> is the centrifugal tension in N, which pulls on the belt even when it carries no load; m is the mass per metre length in kg/m; v is belt speed in m/s; ρ is belt material density in kg/m³; b is belt width in m; t is belt thickness in m.

figure.caption: All three families do the same job but grip differently. Belts cover flat, V, round and timing types; the V-belt wedges into its groove on two sloping sides, which is why it dominates short industrial drives.

spec.aria: A tree of flexible drives under one root with three leaves: belt (flat, V, round, timing; friction or teeth), chain (no slip) and rope (tension only).

examples.question: A leather belt is 100 mm wide and 6 mm thick and runs at 15 m/s over a cast-iron pulley. Take the density of leather as 1000 kg/m³. Find the mass per metre length of the belt and the centrifugal tension set up in it.
steps: Convert to SI: width b = 100 mm = 0.1 m; thickness t = 6 mm = 0.006 m; speed v = 15 m/s; density ρ = 1000 kg/m³.
Volume of one metre of belt = b × t × 1 m = 0.1 × 0.006 × 1 = 6 × 10⁻⁴ m³.
Mass per metre length m = ρ b t = 1000 × 0.1 × 0.006 = 0.6 kg per metre.
Centrifugal tension T<sub>c</sub> = m v² = 0.6 × (15)² = 0.6 × 225 = 135 N.

The belt carries this 135 N on both strands whether or not it transmits power. In the flat-belt design that follows, it is added to the tight-side tension before the strength check, and it plays no part in the friction ratio e<sup>μθ</sup>, so it never helps transmit torque.
examples.answer: Mass per metre length = 0.6 kg/m and centrifugal tension = 135 N.
examples.check:
rho = 1000.0   # kg/m3
b = 0.100      # m
t = 0.006      # m
v = 15.0       # m/s
m = rho * b * t
Tc = m * v**2
print(round(m, 6))
print(round(Tc, 6))

traps: Assuming a V-belt grips on its flat bottom face. It grips on the two sloping sides; the bottom must clear the groove bottom, or the wedge action is lost.
Forgetting that centrifugal tension grows as the square of speed: 15 m/s to 30 m/s takes T<sub>c</sub> from 135 N to 540 N, not 270 N.
Using a friction value without stating it. Leather on cast iron is taken as μ = 0.25 to 0.4; write down the value you use and keep it for the whole problem.
Applying the belt-friction ratio e<sup>μθ</sup> to a timing belt. It drives by tooth engagement, and its rating comes from the teeth, not from friction.
Ignoring the joint. The allowable tension is multiplied by a joint efficiency, and a laced joint is weaker and heavier than a cemented one.

quiz.q: Name the three families of flexible drives and give one member of each.
quiz.a: Belts (flat, V, round, timing), chains (roller, silent) and ropes (wire, fibre).

quiz.q: State the density of leather and the coefficient of friction for leather on a cast-iron pulley, as used in standard belt design.
quiz.a: Density about 1000 kg/m³; coefficient of friction 0.25 to 0.4.

quiz.q: Why are the tension cords of a belt placed near the neutral axis?
quiz.a: Bending stress is proportional to distance from the neutral axis. Cords there see almost no bending stress while carrying the full direct pull, so the belt survives small pulleys and many reversals.

quiz.q: Why is the groove angle of a V-belt pulley made smaller for small pulleys?
quiz.a: When a V-belt bends round a small pulley, its stretched top narrows and its squeezed bottom widens, so the sides close to an angle below 40°. A narrower groove (down to 34°) keeps full side contact and the wedge action; large pulleys use 38°.

quiz.q: A rubber-fabric belt is 120 mm wide and 8 mm thick, density 1100 kg/m³, and runs at 20 m/s. Find the mass per metre and the centrifugal tension.
The same 100 mm × 6 mm leather belt of density 1000 kg/m³ is now run at 30 m/s instead of 15 m/s. Find the new centrifugal tension and compare with 135 N.
quiz.a: m = 0.6 kg/m still. T<sub>c</sub> = 0.6 × 30² = 540 N, four times the 135 N at 15 m/s, because T<sub>c</sub> varies with v².

quiz.q: A machine needs an exact 2:1 speed ratio over a 1.5 m centre distance at moderate power, with no lubrication service available. Choose between a flat belt, a chain and a timing belt, and justify.
quiz.a: A flat belt slips, so the ratio is only approximate — reject. A chain is exact and suits 1.5 m, but needs lubrication and gets noisy at speed. A timing belt is exact, oil-free and quiet at this centre distance. Choose the timing belt; take the chain only if torque is high or the drive is hot and dirty.

quiz.q: A cheap V-belt is run on a pulley whose grooves have worn deeper and wider. Explain what happens to the drive.
quiz.a: The belt sinks until its bottom touches the groove bottom. Contact moves from the two sloping sides to the flat bottom, the wedge factor 1/sin β is lost, and the effective friction drops to about μ. The belt slips, heats and wears fast, and the power it can carry falls sharply.

beyond: Not for the exam. Timing belts now drive printers, engine camshafts and CNC axes, where a quiet, oil-free belt replaces a gear pair or a chain. Aramid and carbon cord belts carry torques that leather could not. Plants check belt health by vibration measurement and infrared thermography rather than by eye. Search "synchronous belt drive" and "belt condition monitoring" to go further.
